segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But know this: in the last days hard times will set in.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: heartless, implacable, slanderous, without self-control, savage, with no love for what is good,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: treacherous, reckless, puffed up with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: holding to an outward form of godliness but having denied its power. Avoid these people as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For among them are those who worm their way into households and take captive weak-willed women who are loaded down with sins and led by all kinds of desires,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: always learning and never able to arrive at knowledge of the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth: people whose minds are corrupted, who have failed the test where the faith is concerned.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they will make no further progress, for their folly will be plain to everyone, as the folly of those two also came to be.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you have followed closely my teaching, my way of life, my purpose, my faith, my patience, my love, my endurance,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: my persecutions, my sufferings, the kind that happened to me in Antioch, in Iconium, in Lystra, the kind of persecutions I endured. And from all of them the Lord rescued me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Indeed, all who want to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: while evil people and charlatans will progress from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as for you, remain in what you have learned and become convinced of, knowing from whom you learned it,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and that from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Every scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that the person who belongs to God may be complete, completely equipped for every good work.

notes.note: The Greek is a diminutive of 'woman' used with contempt, literally 'little women'. It describes the particular women these teachers targeted, not women in general. English versions vary between 'silly', 'weak', 'gullible' and 'weak-willed'; the following phrases about sins and desires suggest that moral weakness is meant, not lack of intelligence.

These names do not appear in the Old Testament. Jewish tradition gave them to the Egyptian magicians who matched Moses' signs before Pharaoh (Exodus 7–9) until their powers failed and they were exposed. The author assumes his reader knows the story.

The word describes something that has been tested and found not genuine, as with coinage or metal that does not pass assay. 'Reprobate' now suggests general depravity, which the Greek does not say. Most modern versions use 'disqualified' or 'rejected', which express the same idea.

In a list of personal qualities alongside patience and endurance, the word could equally mean 'faithfulness', that is, Paul's reliability. Most translations keep 'faith', and the Greek does not settle the question.

notes.phrase: in Antioch, in Iconium, in Lystra
notes.note: These are three cities in the south of Asia Minor where, according to Acts 13–14, Paul was driven out, threatened with stoning, and finally stoned and left for dead. Acts 16:1 places Timothy at Lystra, so these are events he would have known about from his own home region. The Antioch meant is Pisidian Antioch, not Antioch in Syria.

The word originally meant a sorcerer or enchanter, and by this period was commonly used for a swindler or fraud. Most translations choose 'impostors'. 'Charlatans' is used here because it keeps the suggestion of bogus powers, which fits the comparison with Pharaoh's magicians in verse 8; whether actual magical practice is alleged is uncertain.

notes.traditional: of whom thou hast learned them
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts have a plural here, meaning 'from which people', which probably takes in Timothy's mother and grandmother (1:5) as well as Paul. Many later manuscripts have the singular, pointing to Paul alone. English cannot show the difference without paraphrase.

notes.traditional: All Scripture is inspired by God and profitable
notes.note: The Greek has no verb 'is' and no article, so two questions arise. The phrase can mean 'every scripture', passage by passage, or 'all Scripture' as a whole; and the sentence can be read 'every scripture is God-breathed and useful' or 'every God-breathed scripture is also useful'. Most translations and scholars take the first construction, as here, and many prefer 'all Scripture'; the practical difference is small, since the writings in view are the sacred writings of verse 15.

notes.traditional: inspired by God; given by inspiration of God
notes.note: This rare compound joins 'God' and 'breathe' and occurs only here in the New Testament. 'Inspired' comes from the Latin translation and in modern English suggests artistic brilliance, whereas the Greek says that the writings come from God's breath. Several modern versions render it 'God-breathed' or 'breathed out by God'; the word states the origin of scripture without explaining how this happened.

notes.phrase: the person who belongs to God
notes.note: The Greek word is the general one for a human being, not the word for a male. 'Man of God' is also a title in the Greek Old Testament for figures such as Moses and Elijah, and it is applied to Timothy in 1 Timothy 6:11. Many scholars therefore think the phrase here refers especially to Timothy as a Christian leader, while others take it of any believer; the rendering leaves both open.

The Greek uses two words from the same root, an adjective meaning fit or complete and a verb meaning to fit out fully. The repetition in English reproduces this echo. The adjective describes being fully suited to a task, not moral perfection.
